turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): I've done Graham's obs. Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 74, oxygen sat 97 percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks for that. Come on through, Graham. What's brought you in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): It's this cough, doctor. I don't know, it's just been hanging around and it's annoying.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been at it for weeks. Dry as anything, especially in the evening.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): When you cough, are you bringing anything up?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing. No phlegm. Just a tickle that won't quit.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I don't think so. I haven't felt hot.
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hasn't been feverish. I'd have noticed.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your breathing, any shortness of breath?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No, I'm alright getting around. It's just the cough.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): When do you reckon it kicked off?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe three weeks? I thought it was from a cold.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's been five weeks, easy. It started just after we drove up to my brother in Geelong.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Did it? I had a runny nose for a few days back then and that cleared up. The cough stuck around.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the sniffles settled, and the dry cough carried on, worse in the evenings. The timing's wobbly between you, roughly three to five weeks. I'll come back to that.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're on something for your blood pressure. What are you actually taking?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, they started me on a new one. Ramipril, I think. Or was it enalapril? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0019] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's ramipril, five milligrams once a day for his blood pressure, and he started it a few weeks back. Enalapril was never his, that was Uncle Ray years ago. My brother takes lisinopril, but that's not Graham's tablet.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Right, ramipril, for the blood pressure. Yeah. I don't know, the cough seemed to turn up around then. Could still be the cold, I reckon.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you been taking the ramipril every day?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): I think so. Most days. I might've missed one or two. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0023] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's pretty good with it. I see him take it at breakfast.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Speaking of that drive to Geelong, it was a shocker. The ring road was absolutely choked.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about it. I was stuck out that way on Saturday. Took an age just to crawl past the West Gate.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): We had the cricket on in the car. The Aussies were all over them for a bit.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Until that collapse after tea. I nearly turned it off.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): And the weather, stinking hot. Air con on the whole way. You could've fried an egg on the dash.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, probably. Anyway, let's get back to you, Graham.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll have a listen to your chest if that's alright.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear. No wheeze, no crackles. And your throat's not red.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): That's something, I suppose. I don't know what I was expecting you'd find.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): The blood pressure today was 152 over 88, still a bit high for someone already on treatment. Pulse 74, oxygen 97, I'm not concerned about those.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Dry cough, roughly three to five weeks, you don't quite agree on the start, worse in the evenings, no phlegm, no fever, no shortness of breath. A runny nose for a few days that cleared. Ramipril five milligrams once a day for the blood pressure, started a few weeks ago, and you may have missed a dose or two.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's about it. I don't know, doctor, I just want the cough to go. I keep blaming the cold.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had a google and now he's sure the tablet did it. I told him to stop reading that stuff.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can see why you'd both wonder. A dry cough can show up with ramipril, and it can also just be the tail end of a cold. I can't say for certain which this is, and I'm not going to pin a diagnosis on the cough today.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): So you don't know either?

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not firmly, no. What I'd like to do is stop the ramipril and switch you to candesartan, eight milligrams, once a day, for the blood pressure. If the cough is from the ramipril it often settles after a change. If it was the cold, it may ease anyway.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is candesartan the same sort of thing? My brother's lisinopril, that's a different one, isn't it?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Different group. Lisinopril sits with ramipril. Candesartan doesn't. We're not putting you on your brother's lisinopril.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Do I start it tonight? I don't know, doctor, I've still got half a box of the ramipril at home.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the ramipril from today. Don't take any more of those. Start the candesartan tomorrow morning, one eight-milligram tablet, once a day. I'll do the script.
[SEG0044] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if he's still coughing his head off?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Give it time. I'd like to see you back in four weeks, to check the blood pressure and see where the cough is.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the cough gets worse, or you get short of breath, come back sooner, don't wait out the four weeks.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Alright. What about side effects? I don't know, doctor, new tablets make me nervous.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): If your face or tongue swells, that's uncommon but you go to emergency. And if you feel dizzy the first few days, sit down and let me know.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Okay. I'll try not to worry.
[SEG0050] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll stick the ramipril box up in the cupboard so he doesn't take both by mistake.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. One tablet only, the candesartan. Not both.
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): Did you want me to print a path form, or are we leaving bloods?
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): No bloods today, thanks. We'll leave tests for now.
[SEG0054] person_3 (PATIENT): So no chest x-ray? I don't know if I should have one.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not on what I've heard today. Your chest is clear and you're not particularly unwell. We can rethink it if the cough is still hanging around when I see you in four weeks.
[SEG0056] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll grab the four-week appointment on the way out.
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, four weeks with me. Reception will book it. Look after yourself, Graham.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.reason: High blood pressure is supported, but it was elicited by doctor and confirmed by patient, not solely reported by patient.

omissions.text: Chest examination was stated as lungs clear.
Doctor advised no blood tests today / leave tests for now.
Doctor advised no chest X-ray at this stage because chest is clear and patient is not particularly unwell; reconsider if cough persists at review in four weeks.
